title: Work planning, teams and interfaces
moduleTitle: Shared: Growing and managing a team
audience: Any worker in any home-service business in the academy, working under supervision.
learningOutcomes: Explain the boundary for work planning, teams and interfaces and identify when work must stop.
Prepare a task-specific, documented decision for work planning, teams and interfaces under company and local requirements.

instruction.heading: Why planning is a safety control
instruction.body: Many incidents on a job site happen where two groups of workers meet without agreeing who controls what. Work planning turns a job into a sequence of tasks, names who does each task, and sets the points where work must pause. This lesson covers how to plan a job for a small team, how to share a site with other people and other contractors, and how to set clear authority for stopping and restarting work. The aim is not a long document. The aim is that everyone on the site knows what is happening, when, who is in charge and what would make them stop.

instruction.heading: Build the plan from the approved scope
instruction.body: Start from the accepted scope, not from the client's wish list. List the tasks in the order they must happen, the materials and equipment each task needs, the workers authorised for each task, and the time each task takes. Mark any task that needs a permit, a licence or a specialist, and keep it out of the crew's plan until it is cleared. Include the breaks, drying or contact times that the label or the approved method sets, and the points where the area must be checked before the next task begins. A plan that depends on a task nobody is authorised to do is not a plan.

instruction.heading: Allocate roles and supervision
instruction.body: Name one lead for the job, who holds the authority to start, pause and stop work. Name each worker's task and check that it is within the worker's documented training. A worker who is new, or not yet verified for a method, works under supervision and does not perform a task alone that they have not been signed off for. Brief the whole team before the job starts, and again whenever the plan changes. Record who attended, what was agreed and who holds stop authority.

instruction.heading: Manage interfaces with the site and other contractors
instruction.body: An interface is any point where your work meets another person's work, a building system, an occupant or a shared area. Before work starts, identify the site controller or facilities manager, and find out who else will be working in the same zone, on the same day or nearby. Two tasks that are each safe can be unsafe together: a cleaner working beside a contractor who is spraying, grinding or working at height needs the work sequenced or separated, and the site controller must agree the sequence. Do not assume that simultaneous work is safe. Agree who isolates which area, how it is marked and who restarts work once the other party has finished. Keep a written interface schedule and a list of who can stop and restart each activity, and give a copy to the site controller.

instruction.heading: Worked scenario on shared access
instruction.body: Suppose a maintenance contractor is spraying nearby while cleaners are booked for the same zone. The cleaner does not decide alone to carry on. The response is to hold the start of the cleaning task in that zone, tell the crew lead, and contact the site controller to agree the isolation, the sequence and the exclusion area. The agreement is recorded with the times, the names of the people who agreed it and the restart condition. If the site controller cannot confirm the sequence, the cleaning stays on hold.

instruction.heading: Keep the team within its authority
instruction.body: Planning fails when a team quietly expands the scope. If a client or occupant asks for an extra task on the day, do not add it to the plan on the crew's own judgement. Return to the lead and the approver, and update the plan only once the new task has been checked against the worker's training, the approved methods and any licence or permit it needs. Record every change with the reason and the person who approved it.

instruction.heading: Licence notice
instruction.body: Licence notice: This lesson does not grant any licence, permit or authority to perform regulated work, and coordinating work on a site does not authorise any task within it.

instruction.heading: Stop-work rule
instruction.body: Stop and tell the lead immediately if another party starts work that is not in the agreed sequence, if an isolation or exclusion area has been removed, if a person enters the zone without the required briefing, if the task moves outside the written plan or the worker's authority, or if the lead or site controller cannot be reached when a decision is needed. Make the area safe, keep people out, and do not restart until the person named in the plan gives the restart condition.

procedure: Start from the accepted scope and list each task in the order it must happen.
Record the materials, equipment and time each task needs, and mark any task that needs a permit, licence or specialist.
Name the lead for the job and the authorised worker for each task, and check each worker's training for the method.
Identify the site controller, the facilities manager and any other contractors working in the same zone or at the same time.
Agree the sequence, isolation and exclusion area with the other parties, and record the agreement with names and times.
Brief the team before work starts, and record who attended and who holds stop authority.
Check the plan at each handover point, and stop if the area is not as the plan assumes.
Record any change to the plan, the reason for it and the person who approved it.

workedExamples.situation: A maintenance contractor is spraying nearby while cleaners are booked for the same zone.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What is the first safe action, and who must be told?
workedExamples.reasoning: The first safe action is to hold the start of the cleaning task in that zone, rather than assume the two tasks can run side by side. Tell the crew lead, then contact the site controller to agree the isolation, the sequence and the exclusion area. Record the agreement, the times and the names of the people who agreed, and set the restart condition. Cleaning starts only when the site controller confirms the zone is clear.

workedExamples.situation: Cleaners and maintenance contractors need access to the same restricted area on the same afternoon.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Who decides the order of access, and what is recorded?
workedExamples.reasoning: The site controller or facilities manager decides the order of access, because they control the area and know the other contractors' tasks. The lead agrees the sequence with them and writes it into the interface schedule, with the times, the names of those who agreed, and who holds stop authority for each activity. The cleaners do not enter the area until the agreed time slot opens. Any change is recorded and agreed again before the crew acts on it.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Licence notice: completing this lesson is not a licence, certificate or authority to do regulated or restricted work. Check the licence or authorisation rules for your state or territory, and obtain your employer or site written authorisation before starting any work that is outside your training.

Stop-work rule: stop, make the area safe and tell your supervisor before continuing if the task is outside your training or authorisation, the hazard or the required permission is unclear, or the client asks for work that the work order does not cover.

qualityStandard: The work plan is built from the accepted scope, and tasks that need a licence or permit are kept out of the plan until they are cleared.
Each worker is named only for a task they are documented as trained for, and one lead holds stop authority.
Interfaces with other contractors are agreed with the site controller, and simultaneous work is not assumed to be safe.
The sequence, isolation, exclusion area and restart conditions are recorded, and scope changes are approved before they are added.
summary: Plan from the accepted scope, and keep any task that needs a licence or permit out of the crew's plan until it is cleared.
Name one lead with stop authority, and check that each worker is authorised for the task they perform.
Treat two individually safe tasks as unsafe together until the site controller has agreed a sequence.
Record the interface schedule, the isolation, the exclusion area and who can restart each activity.
Do not expand the scope on the crew's own judgement; approve changes first.

knowledgeChecks.question: Before starting work classified as "Work planning, teams and interfaces", what must you do?
options: Start the work and check hazards as you go, since the client has asked for it and the client has paid a deposit
Accept the task if your past experience with similar jobs was safe and the client has been clear about what they want
Ask the client to sign a waiver so the work can begin and the waiver covers every hazard on site
Identify task-specific unknown hazards, qualifications, permissions and controls; place work on hold until verified.

knowledgeChecks.question: Can a planned restricted task go ahead on the employer's paperwork alone?
options: No. Relevant licences, employer/site authorisation and independent competence verification remain required.
Yes, once the employer gives the go-ahead on the paperwork and the client has agreed to the job
Yes, if the client agrees in writing and the client pays a deposit up front for the job
Only if the work is outdoors and at ground level and the work is short, simple and low risk

knowledgeChecks.question: Can a new worker, or one not yet verified for a method, perform a task alone?
options: Yes, once the supervisor has left the site
No. They work under supervision and do not do a task alone that they have not been signed off for
